note.question: How do infection and mortality risks influence optimal LOS of individual patients?
note.overview: Determining the optimal length of stay (LOS) and posttreatment location is critical for hematology-oncology (blood cancer) patients, who are highly vulnerable to life-threatening infections. Early discharge to home care reduces infection risk, whereas extended hospital observation minimizes mortality risks if an infection occurs. The paper addresses this trade-off by developing LOS optimization models tailored to these patients.

source.quote: Problem definition: Determining the optimal length of stay (LOS) and posttreatment location is critical for hematology-oncology (blood cancer) patients, who are highly vulnerable to life-threatening infections.
We further consider the social optimization problem in which capacity constraints limit the ability of hospitals to keep patients for the entirety of their optimal LOS.
Managerial implications: Our model enables physicians to personalize LOS based on patients’ risk profiles and dynamically adapt to hospital capacity constraints.

source.section: The Capacitated Model: A Hospital
source.quote: To disentangle patient LOS from system capacity, we consider an alternative definition of offered load: the expected number of busy servers in an infinite-server queue.

source.section: The Capacitated Model: A Hospital
source.quote: Our approach mimics the methodology of Bassamboo and Randhawa (2016), who use fluid approximations to optimize scheduling in an overloaded queueing system with impatient customers, albeit with a focus on priori­ tization rather than patient service times as we do here.

We find that, in the optimal solution to the fluid model used to approximate the original stochastic system, each type of patient is discharged at at most two discrete time points, one of which might be equal to zero or to the optimal uncapacitated length of stay.

components.explanation: The ISP algorithm is more elaborate than the heuristic proposed by Ouyang et al. (2020) though it shares a common structure: in both cases, when a patient arrives to a full unit, an index-based policy chooses whether the new patient is admitted or another patient is sped up.

conditions: Under this policy, when the hospital ward is at full capacity and a new patient arrives, the system identifies and discharges the patient with the lowest index ξ(τ) := J′ τ=(1 GT(τ)), where τ is the current hospitalization time.

In contrast, the ISP algorithm uses a data-driven index of ξ(τ) = J ′ τ=(1 GT(τ)), which reflects the predicted marginal increase in mortality risk divided by the predicted expected change in patient LOS (based on the patient’s current state).

We end this section with Corollary 3, observing that, if the reward functions J are increasing up to their optimal threshold τopt, it is never optimal to keep a patient for a full stay unless the patient’s τopt = T.
